Part 1 of 2 -- slides 287-298, 8 question(s): covered (confidence 0.95)

The slide set for Topic 21 (slides 287‑298) provides a comprehensive treatment of container orchestration that directly addresses all eight student questions. 

•  The definition of a container orchestrator and the problem it solves is given in slide 289, where the role of scheduling and orchestration is explained. 
•  Slide 292 lists the full suite of tasks automated by orchestration—deployment, configuration, scheduling, resource allocation, networking, scaling, load‑balancing, monitoring, security, and migration—covering the question on automated tasks. 
•  Cluster management is introduced in slide 290, describing how multiple nodes are joined into a fault‑tolerant group and the immutable‑infrastructure model. 
•  The comparison of tools (Docker Swarm, Kubernetes, Amazon ECS, Google Container Engine) appears in slides 294‑295. These slides give clear trade‑offs and specific differences, answering the questions about choosing a tool, the ECS vs. GKE differences, and the Swarm vs. Kubernetes comparison. 
•  Pods are defined in slides 297‑298, explaining why containers are grouped together (shared storage, network, IP, scheduling) and detailing the lifecycle and states of a pod. 

No additional context beyond the topic’s own slides is required to answer the matched questions, and the deck’s internal organization naturally places related content together. Therefore, the topic’s slides adequately cover the student questions with sufficient depth and clarity.

Part 2 of 2 -- slides 298-302, 6 question(s): covered (confidence 0.90)

The slides for Topic 21 (298‑302) provide a comprehensive overview that directly addresses all six matched student questions. 

• The Service section explains what a Service is, why it is needed (to provide stable virtual IPs and load‑balancing for dynamic Pods), and how it tracks changing Pod IPs. 
• The architecture slides describe the master‑node/worker‑node distinction, listing the key components (kube‑apiserver, etcd, kube‑scheduler, kube‑controller‑manager on the master; kube‑let, kube‑proxy, container runtime on workers). 
• The kube‑proxy and kube‑let descriptions are explicit, covering their roles in networking and pod execution. 
• The introductory “Kubernetes Functioning” paragraph gives a functional definition of Kubernetes as an orchestration tool that manages container lifecycles based on declarative configuration.

All questions are answered within the topic’s own slide range, with no need to look beyond the boundary. Therefore the deck’s coverage for this topic is complete and coherent.
